transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 min
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Martin Chen (LedgerGrid - Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (LedgerGrid - Platform), Tom Brooks (LedgerGrid - Security), Elena Park (LedgerGrid - Product)

Summary: Quick product walkthrough of Redwood API, Console, and Optimize focused on edge cases: long context documents, high TPS loads, streaming backpressure and timeout behavior. Demo included live console views and a short benchmark discussion.

Topics covered: long context (32k/100k), high TPS load handling, streaming chunking/backpressure, timeouts and retry policies, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, security controls (VPC/KMS/SOC2).

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna run through some edge cases you mentioned in the intake form — long context, high TPS, and streaming backpressure — hope that's still the agenda.
[00:00:07] Martin Chen: yes, thanks jordan, that's right. we have a couple of production use cases where we stitch together 100k-ish tokens of history and still need low latency for short queries.
[00:00:12] Jordan Lee: cool. i'll hand it to priya for the technical demo, i'll jump in for product and pricing bits.
[00:00:18] Priya Nair: hi everyone, quick note — i'll demo the console and then show a couple of traces. first, long-context: we support 32k natively on some of our curated models, and we have a multi-shard approach for >32k up to ~100k, but there are tradeoffs.
[00:00:30] Sofia Alvarez: multi-shard meaning split across gpus? how does kv cache work across shards?
[00:00:34] Priya Nair: yeah so we shard sequence dimension across GPUs; KV cache coordinates with a distributed cache — we keep a per-shard KV and a routing layer that stitches keys. that can introduce memory pressure and more inter-GPU traffic, so latency can increase for very long contexts.
[00:00:46] Tom Brooks: can you quantify the latency impact? like 1k tokens vs 100k tokens?
[00:00:50] Priya Nair: rough numbers — for a single token step on a 32k window it's similar to standard runs; at 100k we often see 2x-4x token latency depending on model size and hardware. again depends on batching and whether prefix caching is hot.
[00:01:02] Martin Chen: by 2x-4x you mean per-token or end-to-end generation latency?
[00:01:06] Priya Nair: per-token; end-to-end is compounding. also, if you use prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts we can keep hotspots cached and reduce work. it's a big win for chat-like histories.
[00:01:18] Jordan Lee: i'll show the console — (screen share) — here's a demo of a 50k token doc — note the memory gauge, we show shard utilization and the routing logs.
[00:01:28] [00:01:30] Jordan Lee: the console shows cache hit rate, eviction stats — you can tune TTL for cached prefixes.
[00:01:36] Elena Park: is eviction LRU? can we pin certain prefixes?
[00:01:40] Priya Nair: eviction is LRU by default; we also support pinning for specific customer sessions in Dedicated. that's useful for a small set of hot users or documents.
[00:01:50] Sofia Alvarez: ok good. next, high TPS: our production requirement is roughly 1k-3k short requests per second with occasional spikes; we also have batched embed jobs. what do you recommend — hosted or dedicated?
[00:02:02] Jordan Lee: for steady 1k-3k we generally recommend Dedicated pools — predictable throughput and isolated capacity. Hosted can handle spikes but cost becomes variable; we also provide routing policies to fall back to cheaper variants.
[00:02:14] Martin Chen: what about autoscaling on Dedicated — how quickly do you scale?
[00:02:18] Priya Nair: autoscaling is configurable. for short-lived spikes we recommend pre-warming burst capacity; the autoscaler uses a combination of utilization and queue depth signals — typical scale-up is in the order of minutes, not seconds. for millisecond SLOs you use reserved capacity plus burst.
[00:02:33] Tom Brooks: latency SLOs are critical for us. how do you handle streaming backpressure? if client can't read as fast as server streams, do you buffer indefinitely?
[00:02:41] Priya Nair: good question — we don't buffer unbounded. we use a backpressure window: the server streams chunks and maintains a bounded write buffer; if the client can't keep up we apply backpressure to the serving runtime which reduces batch size and can route to asynchronous paths. worst case, we cut the stream and surface a partial result with a specific error code, or fall back to a lower-cost sync response.
[00:03:01] Jordan Lee: practically most of our customers implement a client-side reader with a re-try and resume token; we also support chunked resume points in the API so you can resume from last chunk id.
[00:03:10] Martin Chen: resume token, ok. what's the timeout strategy? our infra has a 30s HTTP gateway timeout for client connections.
[00:03:16] Priya Nair: we recommend keeping streaming responses under the gateway timeout by sending heartbeats/chunks within that window; additionally we have a streaming keepalive you can enable. for longer jobs you should use an async job model where we return a job id and you poll or get a webhook when ready.
[00:03:29] Sofia Alvarez: can the streaming keepalive be disabled — we have strict gateway restrictions.
[00:03:33] Jordan Lee: yes and you can switch to polling or webhooks — the console has a toggle. in Dedicated you can also extend connection timeouts at the load balancer if you control the infra.
[00:03:43] [00:04:00] Priya Nair: switching to the Optimize module — we have recommendations for batching and quantization based on observed token length distribution. for example, for high TPS of short queries batching aggressively gives ~3-5x throughput improvements, but batching increases tail latency.
[00:04:13] Martin Chen: do you have automatic batching or is it client-side?
[00:04:16] Priya Nair: both — runtime supports continuous batching automatically; you can tune batch windows per route. the SDK also exposes batching primitives. Optimize can suggest batch window settings based on your traffic profile.
[00:04:28] Elena Park: any gotchas with quantization? we saw some regression in safety prompts when using int8 on one of our models.
[00:04:34] Priya Nair: yes quantization can affect output quality — Optimize runs eval suites and flags regressions tied to prompts. we recommend a small eval set for safety-critical prompts before enabling aggressive quantization.
[00:04:45] Tom Brooks: security — SOC2, KMS, VPC — we need network diagrams and audit log retention details.
[00:04:52] Jordan Lee: absolutely, we'll share SOC2 and the network diagram. Dedicated and Private give you VPC peering and customer-managed KMS; audit logs are available with retention options. we can also redact transient PII from logs if needed.
[00:05:03] Martin Chen: what about data residency — can workloads be pinned to eu-west-1?
[00:05:07] Jordan Lee: yes, region pinning is supported for Dedicated and Private; Hosted gives region selection but not strict geo-fence unless on an enterprise contract.
[00:05:16] [00:06:00] Priya Nair: jumping back to high TPS specifics — earlier we mentioned continuous batching and cache. for synthetic tests we typically run short-request microbenchmarks at 1k RPS on a dedicated small cluster and then scale. in your case (1k-3k), we'd propose a reserved pool sized for your p95 latency SLO and a burst buffer for spikes.
[00:06:18] Martin Chen: could you run a runbook test for us — simulating 3k steady-state and a 10k spike?
[00:06:22] Priya Nair: yes, that's in scope for the POC. we'll instrument traces and provide flamegraphs. we'll also look at queue depths and batch sizes.
[00:06:30] Jordan Lee: note that for long-context reads, throughput drops — in our bench when context increased from 4k to 50k tokens throughput for short followups dropped ~60% unless hot prefixes were cached. so the POC should mix long-context and short followups to mimic production.
[00:06:45] Sofia Alvarez: makes sense. what about retry behavior when timeouts happen mid-stream — do you support idempotency or is it on the client?
[00:06:51] Priya Nair: we expose idempotency keys for sync calls; for streams we support resumable chunk ids and server-side partial persistence to allow resumed reads. if you must retry a generation idempotently, we recommend using the job API which is retry-safe.
[00:07:05] Tom Brooks: audit logs — are token contents stored? we need to prove no PII retention beyond X days.
[00:07:11] Jordan Lee: default hosted logs keep metadata but you can opt into full transcript logging; Dedicated/Private gives you control over retention and we support bringing-your-own-logging to a customer storage bucket.
[00:07:22] Martin Chen: cost ballpark for Dedicated for our 1-3k RPS?
[00:07:26] Jordan Lee: pricing depends on model family and GPU class; rough ballpark — reserved pool starting in mid-five figures/month for predictable throughput, plus usage for bursts. we'll send a tailored quote after the POC sizing.
[00:07:38] [00:08:00] Priya Nair: ok demo time — showing a live streaming session where we generate a summary of a 50k token doc. note the stream emits chunks every ~200-400ms and the client processes them.
[00:08:10] Priya Nair: (demo) you'll see under load the chunk cadence drops as batch size reduces — the console shows backpressure alerts.
[00:08:18] Martin Chen: i see an error code in the stream 'STREAM_OVERFLOW' — what's that?
[00:08:23] Priya Nair: that's our transient backpressure code — it means the client couldn't accept data fast enough and the server trimmed the connection. the SDK will surface this and optionally provide a resume token if the chunk was partially delivered.
[00:08:33] Sofia Alvarez: are these error codes stable across SDK versions?
[00:08:36] Jordan Lee: yes we maintain a stable set, and breaking changes are versioned in the SDK.
[00:08:40] [00:09:00] Priya Nair: switching to the traces — here's a 3k RPS run we did earlier: you'll see queue depth spikes and batch size reduction. p95 latency held under 300ms for short requests when no long-context anchors are present; when 25% of requests had a 50k prefix p95 jumped to ~900ms.
[00:09:16] Martin Chen: interesting. can Optimize recommend batch windows to avoid p95 spikes?
[00:09:20] Priya Nair: yeah Optimize will analyze distribution and suggest per-route batch windows and model variants; also quantify unit-cost tradeoffs.
[00:09:29] Elena Park: speaking of model variants — can we route to a cheaper quantized variant for non-sensitive requests automatically?
[00:09:34] Jordan Lee: routing policies support that; you can set by route, by user tier, or by detected input type. auto-fallback to a cheaper variant during overload is also supported.
[00:09:44] Tom Brooks: for compliance we need assurance around quantized model behavior — can Optimize run regression evals on our prompts?
[00:09:49] Priya Nair: absolutely — Optimize will run your evals and flag regressions; we'll surface delta metrics.
[00:09:56] [00:10:00] Martin Chen: ok, any constraints for POC — do you need sample data?
[00:10:04] Jordan Lee: sample prompts, representative traffic profile, and a list of safety-critical prompts would be ideal. also the SAML metadata and IPs for peering if you want dedicated.
[00:10:14] Martin Chen: we can provide traffic traces and a small eval set.
[00:10:18] Sofia Alvarez: question — retries under high load increase load; how do you avoid retry storms?
[00:10:23] Priya Nair: our recommended pattern is exponential backoff with jitter client-side and circuit-breakers at the gateway. the runtime also exposes bulkhead patterns that isolate noisy routes.
[00:10:33] Jordan Lee: we can also set per-route throttles and quota enforcement to protect core services.
[00:10:40] [00:12:00] Priya Nair: quick note about memory — some customers saw OOMs when naively enabling 100k windows on older GPU types; we recommend heavier quantization + model parallelism for that.
[00:12:09] Martin Chen: which GPU types do you recommend for 100k workflows?
[00:12:13] Priya Nair: A100 80GB or H100 tends to be best; but we also provide kernel-level optimizations for Ampere/Turing variants. we'll include recommended SKUs in the POC plan.
[00:12:24] Elena Park: can we pin sessions to specific nodes for affinity?
[00:12:28] Priya Nair: session affinity is supported in Dedicated to reduce cache misses, yes.
[00:12:33] [00:15:00] Jordan Lee: ok let's surface the explicit next steps so folks are clear.
[00:15:05] Jordan Lee: action 1: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and the recording + slides by tomorrow.
[00:15:12] Jordan Lee: action 2: Priya will run the 3k sustained + 10k spike synthetic test with a mixed long-context/short-request profile and share traces by 2025-06-18.
[00:15:22] Jordan Lee: action 3: Tom to share SAML metadata and the IP allowlist so we can size Dedicated peering by 2025-06-13.
[00:15:30] Tom Brooks: yes we'll get that over.
[00:15:33] Martin Chen: timeline for POC — we prefer 2 weeks for initial run.
[00:15:36] Jordan Lee: 2 weeks is reasonable — we'll propose a kickoff on 2025-06-20 in the follow-up email.
[00:15:41] [00:30:00] Priya Nair: any final technical quick questions?
[00:30:06] Martin Chen: one more — for streaming backpressure, does the SDK have automatic resume logic or is that something we implement?
[00:30:12] Priya Nair: the SDK includes an optional resume handler that will retry with the resume token; for complex flows we recommend combining resume plus server-side job storage.
[00:30:23] Sofia Alvarez: great. thanks, makes sense.
[00:30:27] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and the POC plan.
[00:30:33] Martin Chen: appreciate it. bye.
